A stock split changes the share unit: chart the count, the price and the holding return together

Five charts explain proportional share splits and reverse splits, comparable historical prices, fractional entitlements and the difference between a quote change and an investment return.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Follow one holding through a proportional share split and a later price

Interactive planning lab

Later value of the full mathematical entitlement$9,982.5
Holding return with the split correctly reflected-8.33%

Original CAD example of a proportional stock split or reverse split, followed by a separately selected later market price. New shares per old share equal the entered new-unit count divided by the old-unit count. The mechanical reference price moves inversely, preserving the holding value at the split itself. Full fractional entitlement is retained mathematically; no issuer or broker cash-in-lieu, rounding, fee, payment date, dividend, tax or account treatment is modeled. Quantity displays round to at most six decimals; calculations retain the full precision. No ticker, live price, split announcement or expected return is used.

The central idea

Multiply the new share count by a price on the new-share basis. A proportional split changes the measurement unit; later market movement determines the change in this example’s holding value.

01

Begin with the complete holding, not a price alert

A price alert can show a large fall on the date of a stock split, while the number of shares in the account rises. Reading just one number can create a false impression of the change in wealth. The starting calculation is the complete holding: shares multiplied by the price for that share unit.

This example starts with 121 shares at CAD 90 each, a holding worth CAD 10,890. A hypothetical three-for-two split gives three new shares for every two old shares. The full mathematical entitlement becomes 181.5 new shares.

The SEC’s Investor.gov glossary describes a stock split as increasing the share count without changing shareholders’ equity. The charts apply that proportional concept to original numbers. They do not reproduce a real company’s event or establish what its shares will trade for.

02

Write the ratio in words before multiplying

The calculator always reads a ratio as new shares for old shares. Its quantity multiplier is new divided by old. Three new for two old gives 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5, so 121 × 1.5 = 181.5 new shares.

The mechanical reference price moves in the opposite direction: CAD 90 ÷ 1.5 = CAD 60 per new share. Multiplying 181.5 by CAD 60 gives the original CAD 10,890. The extra share units are accompanied by smaller units of ownership.

A one-for-two reverse split has a multiplier of 0.5. Before any fractional treatment, the same 121 old shares would become 60.5 new shares, with a proportional reference price of CAD 180. The holding again equals CAD 10,890. An increase in the displayed price per share does not, by itself, double the holding value.

03

Compare earlier and later prices on the same share basis

After the default three-for-two split, assume a later market price of CAD 55 per new share. The old CAD 90 quote and the later CAD 55 quote refer to different share units. Dividing 55 by 90 gives a fall of 38.89%, but it ignores the additional shares.

The comparable earlier price is CAD 60 on the new-share basis. Dividing 55 by 60 and subtracting one gives −8.33%. The same result comes from the complete holding: 181.5 × CAD 55 = CAD 9,982.50, compared with CAD 10,890 originally.

The price chart shows both readings. The unadjusted line moves from CAD 90 to the mechanical CAD 60 reference and then to CAD 55. The comparable line restates the earlier point at CAD 60, stays there for the split reference and then moves to CAD 55. These are three teaching points, not a history of market trading or equally spaced dates.

04

Assign the CAD 907.50 change to the correct step

The waterfall begins with CAD 10,890. It adds zero for the proportional split itself. It then subtracts CAD 907.50 for the later change from CAD 60 to CAD 55 across 181.5 new shares. The endpoint is CAD 9,982.50.

The model does not assume the later market price must equal the proportional reference. Buying and selling can move the actual quote. The reference is useful for isolating the change in units; it does not protect the investment from a subsequent loss.

The endpoint remains a market valuation. No shares have been sold in this example, and the waterfall creates no bank deposit. A spending goal still needs its own sale, settlement and transfer plan if investment value is to become available cash.

05

Keep a fractional entitlement separate from a cash receipt

The default 181.5-share result includes half of a new share. It is a mathematical entitlement before any real-world fractional-share treatment. The calculator retains that half share in every value and return calculation.

Investor.gov’s reverse-split explanation notes that some events cash out partial shares. Its fractional-share bulletin also explains that handling differs across brokerage firms. An actual notice can therefore change what remains as shares and what is eventually paid as cash.

Do not silently round 181.5 down to 181 and treat the missing fraction as a loss. Also do not enter CAD 30 as bank cash merely because half a share times the reference price equals CAD 30. Actual treatment, sale price, fees and payment timing need evidence from the event and the account. None is supplied by this illustration.

06

A large raw quote change can coexist with a much smaller holding change

The matrix varies the split ratio and the true holding return after the mechanical adjustment. Its cells deliberately show the unadjusted later quote divided by the old-share quote, minus one. The column heading, rather than that cell, identifies the assumed holding return.

Under a two-for-one split, a genuine 20% increase after the split leaves the new quote at 60% of the old quote: 1.20 ÷ 2 = 0.60. The unadjusted quote comparison therefore reports −40%, even though the full holding rose 20%.

Under a one-for-two reverse split and zero holding return, the new quote is twice the old quote. The raw comparison reports +100%, while the investment value is unchanged under the model. The ratio is doing the work in both examples; neither describes an observed trading opportunity.

07

A split-adjusted price is only one part of a complete return record

This calculator includes one proportional share split and a later price. It excludes dividends, contributions, withdrawals, fees, taxes, foreign exchange and other corporate actions. A price series adjusted for a split alone should not automatically be labelled a complete total-return series.

The example also does not determine a Canadian tax cost base, calculate a taxable gain or decide whether a particular corporate action is taxable. A historical market value is not necessarily the amount paid for the investment. Keep purchase records and the issuer’s action notice beside the quantity and price reconciliation.

Actual reverse splits can occur alongside other developments, and future trading prices can move. The mathematical value-preservation step is not a statement about a company’s financial health, future performance or suitability for a household’s goal.

08

Reconcile the account before changing the financial plan

  1. Confirm whether the notice says new shares for old shares, and record both sides of the ratio.
  2. Reconcile the old quantity with the new entitlement.
  3. Place earlier and later prices on a consistent share basis.
  4. Separate proportional unit changes from later market gains or losses.
  5. Verify any fractional-share adjustment and actual cash payment in the account records.
  6. Update the goal plan using the holding’s available value and cash dates.

The practical purpose is to keep a change in measurement from distorting a saving or spending decision. The displayed share price, the number of units, the value of the holding and the cash available for a bill each need their own place in the record.

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Independent hypothetical CAD prices, quantities and split ratios. These are bookkeeping illustrations, not a company announcement, historical price series, execution quote or forecast. Fractional entitlements are retained mathematically.
